item.title: Mississippi Says It Won’t Bring Criminal Charges in Police Shooting of Toddler
item.description:
The police officer who shot and killed 1-year-old Kohen Wiley while chasing two women accused of shoplifting was justified in shooting at their car as it pulled out of a Walmart parking space in June, the Mississippi Attorney General’s office announced on Monday.

The decision came four months after Hunter Foster, an officer with the Senatobia Police Department, was placed on leave while state authorities investigated his actions. Although he has not been directly named as the officer who fired, Mr. Foster is the only officer among those present that day who was placed on leave.

A letter from Attorney General Lynn Fitch, posted online Monday by the city of Senatobia, stated that her office would not file charges against Mr. Foster or any other officers because there was “insufficient evidence of criminal conduct.” It was not immediately clear if Mr. Foster would return to work in Senatobia, a small city about 30 minutes south of Memphis.

In a brief statement to the public, Ms. Fitch’s office announced it had completed its review and “found the use of force was justified.”

Many details of the incident remained unknown. State authorities did not say if or when they would release body cam footage or other surveillance video of the incident.

It was also unclear what other evidence state authorities had considered. Several witnesses, including Vellesiya Wiley, who was holding her son Kohen when the officer shot him, said as recently as this month that they had never been interviewed by investigators. Ms. Wiley also denied having taken anything from the store, and said she believed the woman she was with had paid for her items at self-checkout.

Video taken by bystanders around the time of the shooting shows at least five officers on foot intercepting a slow-moving vehicle in the close quarters of a parking lot on a Sunday afternoon. The officers, responding to allegations that a woman had stolen a box of diapers and baby clothes, surrounded the car. None of the video shared publicly so far clearly shows the car, or the officers’ actions, when the shots were fired.

Ms. Wiley said she had been holding her son in her arms in the front passenger seat when the driver, Latoya Ferrell, tried to back out of a space and then drive forward. Both women are Black. Mr. Foster is white.

In the hours after the shooting, the Mississippi Bureau of Investigation issued a statement saying police had fired at a vehicle when it drove toward an officer, “almost striking” one.

Ben Crump, a lawyer for the Wiley family, reiterated his calls Monday for law enforcement officials to release video of the incident.

“How can anyone accept that conclusion when Kohen’s family and the public still have not been allowed to see the body-camera footage?” Mr. Crump said in a statement.

“If the footage supports the state’s decision, release it,” Mr. Crump added. “We will not stop fighting until this family gets the truth.”

Reached by phone on Monday, Ms. Wiley wept over the decision.

Martin Zummach, a lawyer for Mr. Foster, said Ms. Fitch’s decision was “expected” and “overdue.”

Veronica Roberson, Kohen Wiley’s grandmother, said on Monday she had learned of the attorney general’s decision when she logged onto Facebook. No state or local law enforcement official had reached out to the family, she said.

Mr. Foster, 33, is a former member of the U.S. Army National Guard and the son of a longtime law enforcement officer. Before joining the Senatobia department in March 2025, Mr. Foster made a name for himself at the DeSoto County Sheriff’s Office, where he won a state award for issuing the most DUI citations of any law enforcement officer in Mississippi in back-to-back years, 2023 and 2024.

Mr. Foster was promoted to sergeant six months into his term at Senatobia. In the last year, he was twice accused of directing racially offensive language toward co-workers on the job, including referring to a Black officer with an expletive, Mississippi Today reported.

Senatobia’s former police chief, Harold Vanderford, who took no action against Mr. Foster in either case, was fired in September, less than two weeks after The New York Times, Mississippi Today and Verite News revealed he had routinely used racist slurs in private texts with a colleague.

Angelica Maze, a Black woman who was serving as a lieutenant in the department, was named Mr. Vanderford’s interim replacement. She did not respond on Monday to a request seeking comment on the attorney general’s decision.

The city of Senatobia released a brief statement on Facebook on Monday, saying it “continues to extend its deepest sympathy to Kohen Wiley’s family and all those affected by this tragedy.”

item.title: The Overseas X Factor That Could Swing Israel’s Election
item.description:
Bar Luzon, an Israeli citizen living in Cambridge, Mass., never considered herself “a political person.” An assistant professor of linguistics and philosophy at M.I.T., she had not voted in an Israeli election since she came to the United States for graduate school eight years ago. But after the events of Oct. 7, 2023, she said, she could no longer sit on the sidelines.

“It feels like the country is not functioning, in a scary way,” Ms. Luzon, 32, said. She cited Israel’s failure to quickly stop the Hamas-led attack, a lack of vision beyond “war until the end of times” and recent efforts to ban Arab parties from the upcoming elections. “I’m very afraid of how racist my government is, how much it hates its own citizens,” she said.

She now plans to vote against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his allies when Israelis go to the polls on Oct. 27. But there’s a catch. Unlike many democracies, Israel does not allow most citizens to vote absentee from abroad. So Ms. Luzon will be canceling classes and crossing an ocean to try to make her voice heard.

She is far from alone in making the trip.

Uriel Guy, a software engineer in New York, recalled that at a Rosh Hashana dinner he attended last month, “out of the seven Israelis there, all of them were going to vote.” It will be Mr. Guy’s first time voting in Israel since moving to New York in 2013. He has asked his siblings there to pick for him among the different opposition parties, because they are the ones “who will have to actually live with the consequences.”

According to the London-based Institute for Jewish Policy Research, some 630,000 Israeli citizens live abroad, the equivalent of about 6 percent of the country’s population. The American-Israel Democracy Coalition, a U.S.-based group helping Israeli voters living elsewhere with logistical support and chartered flights, announced last week that it expected more than 50,000 to return and cast ballots.

In such a tight contest — polls show a dead heat between the governing coalition and its opposition — those voters could prove pivotal.

In 1996, Mr. Netanyahu, who is often referred to by the nickname Bibi, won his first term as prime minister by a single percentage point. One political consultant later chalked up the victory in part to conservative voters who flew in at the time to support him. This past June, Peru’s presidential election was decided by votes from abroad.

What’s more, in a chaotic parliamentary system like Israel’s, small swings can have outsized impacts. In 2022, the parties that made up Mr. Netanyahu’s hard-right coalition won 48.4 percent of the vote but obtained 64 of the parliament’s 120 seats because two anti-Netanyahu parties — one leftist, one Arab nationalist — fell just shy of the electoral threshold for making the Knesset. The government that was in place on Oct. 7 and oversaw Israel’s response to the attack had come to power by the thinnest of margins.

For many who did not vote in Israel’s last election, the events of that day and its aftermath have served as a wake-up call. “Israelis abroad typically lived in their own bubble,” said Jonathan Barsade, president of the AID Coalition, which is nonpartisan in its current messaging but has supported protests against the Netanyahu government in the past. “Since Oct. 7, all of a sudden, they came out of that bubble.”

In theory, far-flung Israelis of any political persuasion could attempt to tilt the electoral outcome by returning to vote. But secular and more educated Israelis, who tend to lean left, are more likely to have moved abroad for work opportunities — or as an act of political protest — and are more likely to be able to afford the trip back. Many of those outside the country are also more aware of and alarmed by its deteriorating international standing.

Yael Shomer, a political scientist at Tel Aviv University, said that Israelis who departed the country in recent years — well over 100,000, according to official data — tended to have advanced degrees and hail from liberal areas, like Tel Aviv.

“The Israeli Central Bureau of Statistics actually analyzes the characteristics of those Israelis who left,” she said, “and we know from other research that those characteristics are correlated quite strongly with center-left leaning voters who support the current opposition parties.” In other words, the composition of the Israeli community abroad has changed, and so has who it benefits when they vote.

In recent interviews with The New York Times and other outlets, many Israelis living elsewhere said they intended to vote against Mr. Netanyahu and his allies.

Among them was Amit Stern, a 51-year-old dual American-Israeli citizen who moved to the United States when he was six and has gone back and forth since. After watching the Hamas attack unfold from his New York living room, he returned to Israel in 2023 to assist his former army unit, patrolling the Gaza border for several weeks. Three years later, Mr. Stern will be returning to cast a ballot against the country’s leadership.

“There is huge dissonance between the Israelis as a population and the government that is managing them,” he said. He hopes that the election will empower a new government composed of “people with more integrity,” he said, not divisive leaders who “scare people, as Bibi often likes to do.”

Some Israelis abroad feel compelled to vote out of civic duty. Others express a deep sense of foreboding about Israel’s future if the country does not change course.

“I have five grandchildren and there won’t be an Israel for them,” said Susan Lax, a co-owner of the Israeli footwear brand Na’ot, who grew up on a kibbutz and lost a friend on Oct. 7. She and her partner split their time between New York and Tel Aviv, and will be returning to Israel to vote against the current coalition.

Guy Ben-Aharon, an Israeli in Boston, is currently deciding between the two main Arab parties, in part because he does not feel that the Jewish opposition parties “speak openly enough against the occupation and the apartheid reality and the war in Gaza,” in which tens of thousands of Palestinians have been killed. “Do I think that a change of regime in Israel is going to change everything I care about?” he said. “Not at all. Do I think it’s important to vote Bibi out? Very much so.”

If the current leadership manages to stay in power, “I’m afraid that thousands of Israelis will leave,” said Danny Peleg, a former Israeli special forces captain living in Boulder, Colo. “Israel will no longer be a democratic state, and I’m afraid that the decisions will be led by a person who has the fear of going to jail” — a reference to Mr. Netanyahu’s ongoing corruption trial — “and wars will continue forever.”

Mr. Peleg and his wife have two children living in Israel, and another who works at an Israeli embassy in Europe. He bought plane tickets as soon as the election was called.

Israelis abroad are not a political monolith.

Ricki Alon, an entrepreneur from Los Altos Hills, Calif., who arrived this week to vote in Israel, said she will vote for Mr. Netanyahu despite significant misgivings. She said she considers him the most qualified to run the country out of the available options, adding that he has “the most experience, ability, and skills to manage this crisis.”

Last month, one former Israeli chief rabbi ruled that religious expats — who tend toward the right — could use certain charity funds to fly to Israel to vote for one party in Mr. Netanyahu’s coalition. But in practice, both the Israeli government and opposition understand that voters abroad these days are most likely to support the challengers.

“When we look at the profile of those coming this time, the profile is liberal Israelis living abroad,” Yaron Deckel, a former regional director of the Jewish Agency, an Israeli nonprofit that operates in 65 countries, said at an Israeli political conference last week.

“That’s why it worries Likud so much,” Mr. Deckel said, referring to Mr. Netanyahu’s party, as opposed to “in the past when ultra-Orthodox Jews from New York came to vote, because they were more identified with parties that support the right.”

Mr. Netanyahu’s allies have criticized efforts to increase international turnout. “The left is now trying to bring in masses of people from abroad,” Shlomo Karhi, Israel’s communications minister, told a radio program in August. “Anyone who doesn’t live here in the country shouldn’t come.”

In May, Mr. Netanyahu’s Likud Party threatened legal action against the AID Coalition, and later filed a petition against it, alleging that the group’s neutral veneer concealed a partisan purpose. Likud withdrew the suit this month after the AID Coalition agreed to several restrictions on its work.

None of these machinations have deterred Ms. Luzon, the M.I.T. professor. “I have to do the only thing I can do, even though its effect is minuscule,” she said. “I want to be there to celebrate if we manage to replace this horrible government.”

And if that fails? “I spent a lot of time crying in the last three years. I’d rather do it with my friends in Israel than do it here alone.”

item.title: A Colorado Town Was Beset by Traffic. Its Fix Led to a Border Battle.
item.description:
When Craig Patterson and his wife moved to the wealthy Denver suburb of Bow Mar eight years ago, they felt safe letting their son and daughter roam its winding, leafy roads. Then cars started crashing into everything.

There was the woman who plowed into a rock wall at the entrance to town. An S.U.V. that rammed a roundabout. The drunk landscaper who took out a pine tree and mailbox a few doors down from the Pattersons.

All were among the many drivers who cut through Bow Mar to avoid clogged main roads. But to a quiet town founded as a bedroom community of Denver in the 1940s, they represent an unwelcome encroachment of the region’s explosive growth that has reached a full-blown border crisis.

Now Bow Mar has an idea: keep out the traffic by gating off its serene streets.

Bow Mar residents have packed town meetings this year in support of gates, calling them a public safety necessity. But critics say Bow Mar, a town of $3 million homes with its own private lake, is trying to escape the downsides of growth by walling itself off — an idea that rankles some in liberal Colorado as a miniature border barrier.

“That fancy little town in the metro area doesn’t want us peasants driving through anymore,” Kyle Clark, a local news anchor, told viewers in a recent segment that first reported on the plans and still has Bow Mar residents angry.

The fight echoes conflicts across the fast-growing Western United States about whether to welcome newcomers or beat them back like invasive weeds. There is a boom in bumper stickers and T-shirts that declare: Don’t California My Arizona (or Texas or Idaho). A jokey new online shop called Wyoming Border Patrol urges a wall to keep Coloradans from migrating north.

While thousands of gated communities across the country have their own privately maintained roads, Bow Mar’s plan to block its public streets would make it the rare gated town. Residents would get radio tags allowing them passage and key codes to give to their guests. Emergency vehicles would also have access.

Bow Mar initially proposed building three gates and closing off an additional public street, but in a statement, the town said that it was gating off only one entry into the town, and that drivers could still take other routes in. The mayor and town trustees declined an interview request.

“This is not an effort to privatize public streets,” the town said in a statement.

The larger cities of Denver and Littleton, which surround Bow Mar, do not see it that way. They say that Bow Mar cannot restrict public streets that are funded in part by state tax dollars.

“It’s hurtful when your neighbor says, You’re not welcome in our community,” said Kyle Schlachter, the mayor of Littleton, a city of 46,000.

Mr. Schlachter said he first learned about the gate plan last winter from a puzzled Littleton resident who had caught wind of the proposal. Littleton and Bow Mar have cooperated on road projects and wastewater treatment over the years, and Mr. Schlachter said he had reached out to Bow Mar to negotiate a non-gate option, such as tougher traffic enforcement or more speed bumps. He said the town had declined.

Mr. Schlachter said he worried any gate could slow emergency vehicles and make other roads even more congested. But more than that, he said, it would be unfair, because Bow Mar’s residents drive on Denver or Littleton streets every time they leave their one-square-mile town.

“They want to be able to use our roads, but they don’t want us to use their roads,” he said. “Do we need to put up gates of our own?”

As the gate debate has ricocheted across the internet, some Bow Mar residents say they have been slandered online as snooty elitists. They have spotted pickup trucks “rolling coal” through town, belching black clouds of diesel smoke.

“We just want to keep our kids safe,” said Dawn Fable, who has lived in the town for 10 years. “They’re not able to play outside. Someone is going to die.”

There have been two crashes in the Fables’ front yard. One happened on an evening last October, when a truck gunning down the road almost hit their 12-year-old son as he changed a bike tire.

The truck crashed into a mailbox across the street, and when Ms. Fable’s husband, Shane, ran out with his phone to record the scene, he found the driver with blood on his face, slurring his words. The man was arrested on charges of reckless driving and vehicular assault for driving while drunk, according a police report.

“I never wanted to live in a gated community,” Mr. Fable said, “but it is out of control.”

Apart from the occasional runaway truck, Bow Mar feels like a suburban Brigadoon.

It is a quilt of sprawling one-story homes sitting on one-acre lots under a canopy of mature ash trees, with no businesses other than a tiny marina along the private lake. During the day, joggers huff along gravel walking trails, and parents in golf carts pick up their children from the bus stop. It has no sidewalks or streetlights, and at night, the streets are swallowed in darkness.

“You move here to let your kid enjoy being a kid,” said Mr. Patterson, the father of two. He said his sense of safety was first jolted about five years ago, when an unfamiliar silver car sidled up alongside his daughter, then 11, as she and a friend walked down the road and the driver tried to lure them in by offering a ride.

Bow Mar says the number of nonresident drivers has soared as metro Denver has exploded over the past decade and new apartment buildings have spread across the suburbs. The town tried lowering the speed limit to 20 miles per hour and installing speed bumps, to no avail.

A traffic study commissioned by the town found that about 2,000 vehicles entered on an average day last year, a roughly 25 percent rise from 2017. The police issued 1,260 traffic violations, half of them speeding tickets, from the start of 2023 through this summer — a big number in a town of just 850 people, 193 of them children under 15.

Some residents have responded to the traffic by planting “SLOW DOWN” signs in their yards, installing boulders along property lines as traffic breaks or hiding GoPro cameras in the bushes. One father is so worried about out-of-control drivers, he said, that he no longer lets his daughters go to the family’s roadside mailbox.

The pro-gate contingency got another data point in their favor last week, when a gray S.U.V. drove into the lake and ended up stuck in three feet of water. A Bow Mar spokesperson said the driver — who appeared to have fled the scene — wasn’t a resident.

When I heard about the kerfuffle over a tiny Colorado town's proposal to gate off its streets, I thought about my time covering the Southern border and the battles over building a wall there. The fight here is obviously much smaller, but the questions were similar. Do barriers work? And how do neighbors get along in this fractious era?

item.title: A.I. Fortunes Could Bring Critical Funds to Global Health. The Scramble Is On.
item.description:
When world leaders gathered at the United Nations in New York last month, there were many somber meetings about how to tackle the crucial problems of global health at a time when governments, led by the United States, have sharply reduced financial support.

But there were also other meetings: small gatherings, in private dining rooms, where new interlocutors grilled veteran leaders of international health organizations with unfamiliar and startling questions: What would you do with another billion dollars? What about $5 billion? What are the “shovel ready” projects that could quickly absorb $100 million or more?

A senior executive, emerging dazed from one of those dinners, described it as “a gold rush,” a frantic scramble as organizations sought to make sure they were in line to grab a share of what is anticipated to be a monumental wave of new funding for health aid.

The source is the wealth coming from the initial public offerings of major artificial intelligence companies, starting as soon as next month. These could put tens of billions of dollars of new philanthropic money in the hands of charities chosen or set up by a new class of ultrawealthy givers, many of whom have a demonstrated interest in global health.

The A.I. windfall, which some are calling a “third wave of philanthropy,” may rival or even exceed the amount given by the governments of wealthy nations.

The new funders bring a tech founder mind-set that could spur ambition, accelerate the introduction of new drugs and tools, and hold sclerotic institutions to new standards of performance.

But these funders tend to have a preoccupation with metrics and results that does not easily graft to the complex work of ending poverty. And as they become some of the most powerful players in the field, the shift could undermine the sovereignty of low-income countries trying to take control of their own health systems after decades of heavy-handed external influence.

“I have a huge amount of optimism that there are large amounts of capital coming in to solve some of the most important problems in the world,” said Dr. Neil Buddy Shah, chief executive officer of the nonprofit Clinton Health Access Initiative, who has become an influential voice with tech executives planning to give away large portions of their coming fortunes. “And that this money is pretty relentlessly focused on trying to chase impact and drive measurable improvements in people’s lives.”

For decades the global health architecture has been structured around wealthy governments that donate to low-income countries reliant on their help, aid agencies that run programs, a few huge multilateral organizations, and a beneficent billionaire, Bill Gates, as an additional playmaker.

Mr. Gates’ foundation will give away $9 billion this year, most of it to global health, the largest amount of philanthropic spending in the world.

The seven co-founders of Anthropic, which is valued at close to a trillion dollars and poised to stage its I.P.O. next month, have pledged to give away 80 percent of their wealth. On Sunday, the company said it will commit five percent of its shares to a new public benefit fund.

The OpenAI Foundation holds 26 percent of OpenAI, which is valued at about $850 billion. OpenAI has already granted roughly $80 billion in vested equity to employees.

Pledged money is not the same as actual donations, however, and concerns about A.I. security could postpone the initial public offerings or lower the companies’ market values. Global health is just one field vying for this money; A.I. security and animal welfare are among other priorities of these new donors.

Many of the new A.I. philanthropists have a background in “effective altruism,” a philosophy that focuses on using data to calculate how to do the most good for as many people as possible. Fifteen years ago, that nascent movement identified the fight against malaria, and in particular the purchase and distribution of anti-mosquito bed nets, as the most cost effective way to save a life.

That highly successful intervention was the gateway to their interest in other relatively low-cost, evidence-backed health measures, such as immunization; deworming; and distribution of oral rehydration salts to treat diarrhea, a top killer of small children.

Effective altruists have been major donors to two large “aggregators,” GiveWell and Coefficient Giving, which research cost-efficient interventions, advise would-be philanthropists and provide a channel for grant making that some entrepreneurs are using even as they start to set up their own foundations.

The new funders bring a Silicon Valley-bred skepticism to their giving, according to health experts who have been asked to advise them. They refer to organizations such as the Gates Foundation as “TradPhil” and are dubious of the large aid agencies, which they see as bloated, inefficient and insufficiently motivated by evidence.

“The way technologists look at problems is, We know how to fix this, you program this,” said Wendy Schmidt, who with her husband, Eric Schmidt, the former head of Google, launched a global health charity last week. Ms. Schmidt said she is learning that there is no substitute for the input of development veterans. “It’s not simple, it’s not an algorithm, you have to get your feet dirty and be on the ground.”

The biggest signal of the scale and implications of this funding shift is a proposed donation of $2 billion to $3 billion to the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria. The United States, the Fund’s largest donor, gave $1.65 billion last year.

The money is being offered through GiveWell, which would not disclose the identity of the donors making the new offer. But internal Global Fund documents obtained by the Times describe it as a “potentially transformative new source of private philanthropic financing.”

The money would go to fighting malaria in countries where the disease exacts its highest toll. The Global Fund’s board will vote next week on whether to create a new “Malaria Impact Accelerator” as the vehicle for GiveWell’s investment.

In the documents outlining the terms of the deal to the Global Fund board, the organization’s executives said the arrangement would give a donor unprecedented power to decide what interventions a country will use, upending the model the Global Fund has used for nearly 25 years, and noted that the amount and duration of the support is uncertain, tied to a volatile industry.

But those risks are worth taking, they urged the board, to be at the front of the line. “The donor is taking decisions now about which channels to utilize to invest in the fight against malaria, to begin deploying financing as rapidly as possible as soon as it becomes available,” they wrote, and warned that if the fund doesn’t accept the terms, the donor will quickly move on.

While the broader trend in global development in recent years has been to help countries strengthen their health delivery systems, and to move away from programs that focus on a single disease, like tuberculosis or H.I.V., that approach does not fit as well with the kind of impact assessment that effective altruism demands.

A veteran program manager who has been fielding calls to advise new funders said the vision they describe is like a stock ticker, an app on their phones that shows a steadily rising total of children immunized or vitamin A doses delivered.

The head of a large health aid organization who is courting A.I. executives, and who would not speak on the record because those talks are ongoing, said he has seen their attitudes shift as they start to learn more about the complexities of health care delivery in war zones and countries with fragile governments. Where they initially had a “strip everything down, crash out, reinvent” mind-set associated with tech start-ups, they have come to see that the initial approach may not be as effective in this field, he said.

Alexander Berger, the chief executive of Coefficient Giving, said he urges new donors to be open to working with existing large institutions such as the Global Fund and Gavi, which helps low-income countries procure immunizations. They have a proven track record of delivery, he said, and creation of many organizations working on overlapping issues could dilute their impact.

Jacob Trefethen, who heads a division of the OpenAI Foundation focused on life sciences and curing diseases, said there is room for some positive disruption in the field. “We’re trying to think really carefully about which problems we should seed new organizations around and when we should work with established players,” he said. “We’ll do a mix of both.”

His organization, and the aggregators, are rapidly expanding their staffs, bringing on experts from organizations such as the Gates Foundation and the Center for Global Development as they prepare to accelerate the amount of money they move.

The foreign aid cuts of 2025 left gaping holes in the health care systems of many developing countries; redirected domestic resources have plugged only part of the gaps. But some governments say that the slim upside is increased control over their own health spending priorities. The new class of donors could reverse that fragile trend.

There are also big questions about whether the influx of new money may lead donor countries, including the United States, to reduce contributions further, thinking the new A.I. money will pay what’s needed to fight malaria or immunize children. “That’s a major risk that we see here, the feeling among the donor governments that they can really pull back without harm,” said Elie Hassenfeld, the chief executive officer of GiveWell.

The interventions that the new effective altruist-influenced donors like best — the ones that perform well when evaluated on metrics like “net benefit for each marginal dollar spent” — require health systems to deliver them. But building a better primary health care system is long-term work, where positive changes are more difficult to measure empirically.

Dr. Shah, who chairs Anthropic’s Long-Term Benefit Trust, said he is encouraging would-be donors to think more broadly about what “effective” can mean in global health. Yes, he tells them, you should count lives saved or illness prevented. But, he argues, there is a beneficial side effect in strengthening the health system that doesn’t show up as neatly on the balance sheet.

Yet, said Mr. Trefethen from OpenAI Foundation, “I think this new influx of money might get us, in the long run, to a more sustainable and more just future.”

“There will be issues and learning along the way,” he conceded. “But when new resources are directed with the intention of benefiting some of the least resourced people on earth, it’s hard not to feel more enthusiastic.”

Theodore Schleifer contributed reporting.

I laughed out loud the first time I heard the phrase “TradPhil” from a source, but the snarky term speaks to a critical question: Is the current global health system ripe for disruption? New players are bringing a critical infusion of cash, and that’s going to give them power to call the shots — even if they know very little about the complex business of trying to save lives in the world’s poorest places.

item.title: Taunting Trump Over Gas Prices, Iran Braces for Aftermath of U.S. Vote
item.description:
In the run-up to the midterm elections, Iranian state media is gleefully chronicling high prices at American gas pumps — and their impact on President Trump’s political standing.

Outlets like Tehran’s semiofficial Fars News Agency cite polls reflecting voter anger at Mr. Trump over his conflict with Iran.

Iranian officials are piling on. In an open letter to Americans last month, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps wrote that Mr. Trump “keeps on telling Americans that the economy is booming and the prices will soon start coming down,” adding: “This is, perhaps, his biggest lie.”

A few days earlier, the speaker of Iran’s Parliament, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, mocked a spike in U.S. Treasury bond rates. “We’ll return you to 1970s rates, plus high gas prices, diesel shortages and bell-bottoms. Enjoy the nostalgia!” he wrote.

Iran’s leaders clearly relish the political damage Mr. Trump has suffered from the conflict he launched in late February, even as their own economy suffers extreme stress from U.S. sanctions and an American naval blockade.

There are signs that political and economic pressure has pulled Mr. Trump back from the brink of military escalation, and the election result could determine what steps the United States takes next.

“They’re desperate to try and affect the election, so that we can get a nice weak group of people in there, and leave them alone and let them have their nuclear weapon,” Mr. Trump told reporters last month.

It is not the first time Iran has been suspected of maximizing political pain against an American president. After Iranian revolutionaries stormed the U.S. Embassy in Tehran and took dozens of Americans hostage in November 1979, U.S. intelligence agencies concluded that Iran was drawing out the crisis “to bring about President Carter’s defeat” in the 1980 election, as a declassified C.I.A. analysis put it that year.

Mr. Carter lost to Ronald Reagan that November, an outcome he publicly attributed, in part, to the hostage ordeal.

For years, Iranian leaders have threatened to kill Mr. Trump, and in March a federal jury convicted a Pakistani national working as an Iranian intelligence agent of entering the United States in 2024 to arrange Mr. Trump’s assassination. Humiliating Mr. Trump in the elections is a way for Iran to get “satisfaction without doing something more drastic,” said Vali Nasr, a professor at Johns Hopkins University’s School of Advanced International Studies.

Iran’s ability to menace the Strait of Hormuz and attack the energy infrastructure of its neighbors has given Iran valuable insights into how it can exert pressure over the United States and the global economy.

That has also probably bought Iran at least some relief from further attacks in recent months by a president wary of military escalation that could drive oil prices even higher and anger voters who already mostly oppose the Iran conflict.

But any satisfaction in Tehran could evaporate quickly. Iranian leaders have grown more concerned lately about what might come after the U.S. elections, analysts said. With two years left in his last constitutionally allowed term as president, Mr. Trump may feel freer after Nov. 3 to take drastic action that could include a major new round of attacks on Iran.

“Once the elections are done, he may be free to do whatever he wants,” said Mr. Nasr, the author of the recent book “Iran’s Grand Strategy: A Political History.”

Iran hawks close to the Trump administration are hopeful that Mr. Trump will carry out new attacks, including on Iran’s already-battered nuclear facilities. The military has developed plans for heavy strikes and has concentrated more forces in the region, and will soon have three aircraft carrier groups positioned there.

“While Trump is unpredictable, there are certainly signs that he might hit Iran hard” after the midterm vote, said Michael Makovsky, the president and chief executive of the Jewish Institute for National Security of America, a hawkish think tank in Washington.

Mr. Trump may hold out “slim” hope for striking a deal before Election Day, Mr. Makovsky added. “But he doesn’t seem to think it’s likely.”

Mr. Trump has both accepted and rejected the idea that electoral politics influence his war plans. Speaking at the United Nations on Sept. 22, he claimed that Iran was the party focused on the U.S. vote, and that it was stalling peace talks.

“I believe we’ll make a deal right after the election,” Mr. Trump said. “They’re waiting to see how I do in the midterm election.”

“I gave absolutely no credence and will not give credence to the election when it comes to Iran; it doesn’t even enter my mind,” he added.

Less than three weeks later, however, Mr. Trump declared on social media that he would not attack Iran “at any time prior to” the November vote.

But Mr. Trump is unpredictable, to say the least, and some analysts believe the opposite might happen. “After the midterms, Trump may no longer feel burdened to pretend to be interested in the Iran war,” Cole Bucy and Nate Swanson, two Iran specialists who have worked on the White House National Security Council, wrote in a Sept. 30 essay in Foreign Policy.

Freed from electoral politics, Mr. Trump “may decide that he can weather the criticism and declare victory, without having to worry about a new forever war to tarnish his legacy,” they wrote.

Mr. Bucy and Mr. Swanson did not rule out the prospect of a major escalation, including a U.S. ground invasion of at least parts of Iran, something they called unlikely.

The ultimate problem for Mr. Trump, Mr. Swanson concluded in an interview, is that “these are all bad options.”

item.title: Aided by Supreme Court Ruling, R.N.C. Pumps $50 Million Into Midterms
item.description:
Taking advantage of a recent Supreme Court decision, the Republican National Committee is sending tens of millions of dollars to help the party’s midterm candidates. The long-awaited move adds to the G.O.P.’s considerable financial advantages, especially in Senate races, despite a tough political environment.

The R.N.C., which entered September with an enormous $126 million on hand, told The New York Times that it was finishing moving more than $50 million to the groups overseeing the party’s efforts to elect House and Senate candidates. The cash infusion, significantly larger than what Republicans have done in the past, is something that the troubled and financially struggling Democratic National Committee is incapable of doing.

The R.N.C. told The Times that it had transferred more than $44 million between mid-August and mid-October to the party’s main House and Senate committees. Many of those transfers will be disclosed for the first time in a campaign-finance filing on Tuesday evening. The cash was about evenly split between the National Republican Congressional Committee, which works to elect House Republicans, and its Senate counterpart, the National Republican Senatorial Committee. At least $6 million more is set to be sent to those two committees by Election Day, the committee said.

The spending comes as Republicans play defense across the midterm map, devoting resources to states and districts that were once thought to be safely red as President Trump’s low approval ratings weigh on the party’s candidates.

The R.N.C. has amassed its huge war chest in part thanks to an aggressive fund-raising effort by Mr. Trump and Vice President JD Vance, who has led the party’s finance operation. The party said it raised $18.5 million in September. By Oct. 14, R.N.C. officials said, its $126 million coffers had been drawn down to $76 million, a campaign-finance filing on Thursday will show.

Transfers are not new. In the four most recent election cycles, the R.N.C. has transferred between $8 million and roughly $31 million to these party committees.

But the shift of money goes much farther this time. In June, the Supreme Court struck down limits on the amount of coordinated spending that party committees could do with candidates. That was a major change, probably the largest in campaign finance since the 2010 Citizens United decision, which lifted limits on corporate spending in elections. And this year’s ruling from the conservative-controlled Supreme Court stood to immediately benefit Republicans, because they have much more money in their party committees.

The Republican House and Senate party committees have been able to channel their money into advertising that is more coordinated with candidates than what their Democratic counterparts are doing.

Those two Capitol Hill committees have aired or booked about $152 million worth of ads through coordinated purchases, according to data from the media-tracking firm AdImpact, the largest being for Senator Jon Husted in Ohio. The R.N.C. itself is airing another $5 million worth of ads that it coordinated with Representative Ashley Hinson’s campaign for Senate in Iowa, a move it doesn’t expect to repeat with other candidates.

All told, Democratic committees have aired or booked only about $102 million worth of such ads, the largest being for Mr. Husted’s opponent, former Senator Sherrod Brown in Ohio.

The Times reported in July that the D.N.C. could not afford to make planned transfers to Democrats’ congressional committees. The D.N.C. has reported holding negative cash on hand, inclusive of its debt, for almost the entire 2025-26 election cycle. Mia Ehrenberg, a D.N.C. spokeswoman, said the committee had made “historic, early, and aggressive investments in critical party infrastructure,” sending over $1 million to state parties each month.

The two parties’ House and Senate committees had relative parity in fund-raising through Aug. 30. That is why R.N.C. officials say that their transfers are responsible for the current Republican advertising advantage in coordinated spending, most of which was booked since that date.

Mike Ambrosini, the R.N.C.’s chief of staff, said the strategy of coordinated spending had been part of his pitch to donors. “We’re moving all this money directly into these campaigns,” he said, “so we felt it was important that folks understood that investing with us meant that your dollar could cover all of those different use cases.”

The R.N.C. is sticking to its traditional work of funding ground game and data work for candidates. Party officials said that through early October, they had spent about $56 million on canvassing and voter-turnout operations, $27 million on “election integrity” work, $18 million on the party’s data operation and about $11 million on digital work.

Party officials were careful to note that the R.N.C. will not spend all of its money on hand in the midterms, and that tens of millions of dollars are likely to be left over. That is because some of the cash is held in special accounts designated for uses like legal fights and building renovations, and are not legally allowed to be used on campaigns themselves.

Still, Mr. Ambrosini said, “there’s no saving money for a rainy day.” He added, “Whatever we can get that can be deployed is going to be deployed.”

item.title: J Street’s Super PAC Targets Two Republicans Backed by AIPAC
item.description:
The super PAC for J Street, a liberal pro-Israel advocacy group, released two ads on Tuesday targeting a pair of Republican members of Congress who have been endorsed by AIPAC.

The ads are the first time J Street’s super PAC has taken on the American Israel Public Affairs Committee in a general election, which has long prided itself on bipartisanship and backed members from both parties. But AIPAC has increasingly become a pariah in some Democratic circles and has faced a backlash after spending millions in Democratic primaries.

One ad criticizes Mariannette Miller-Meeks in Iowa’s First Congressional District and the other denounces Ryan Mackenzie in Pennsylvania’s Seventh Congressional District for their positions on health care and ties to insurance companies.

J Street, which refers to itself as “pro-Israel and pro-peace,” has sought to position itself as an influential player in Democratic politics and on Capitol Hill. The group’s super PAC, J Street Action Fund, has spent $3 million in the midterm campaign. That is a record for J Street, but it is a small fraction of the tens of millions spent by AIPAC’s super PAC, United Democracy Project.

Neither of the new ads explicitly mentions Israel, which organizers say is not the primary issue for the overwhelming majority of voters.

J Street Action Fund this month also released an ad condemning the Republican Senate candidate in Georgia, Mike Collins, for his reported history of hiring aides who have espoused white nationalist and antisemitic views.

“J Street Action Fund’s investment in these targeted races represents the views of a majority of Jewish Americans who understand that we need to preserve American democracy and fight xenophobia in all its forms to keep our communities safe,” Tali DeGroot, the group’s political director, said in a statement.

item.title: Trump Invokes Antisemitic Trope Again at Rally for Kansas Senator
item.description:
President Trump invoked a centuries-old antisemitic trope to defend the aggressive debt-collecting tactics of Senator Roger Marshall, the first-term Republican fighting for re-election in Kansas, before the senator began his political career.

At a rally on Monday with Mr. Marshall in Park City, Kan., the president said Mr. Marshall’s opponents had unfairly cast him as “some kind of a Shylock-type guy,” an apparent reference to recent reporting by The New York Times that revealed that Mr. Marshall had filed lawsuits against more than 700 patients with outstanding medical bills during his decades-long career as an obstetrician-gynecologist. Mr. Marshall, The Times reported, routinely charged an 18 percent annual interest rate and also garnished patients’ paychecks and bank accounts. Mr. Trump did not mention The Times by name.

Shylock is the name of the Jewish moneylender from Shakespeare’s “The Merchant of Venice.” The character, who demands a pound of human flesh as collateral for a loan, has become shorthand for antisemitic representations of avarice and usury.

At the rally, Mr. Trump sought to make the case that Mr. Marshall had been following the law.

“He’s a fine person,” Mr. Trump said of Mr. Marshall, who is not Jewish. “And he was given a bum rap because he was mandated by law to request, strongly, money owed from patients. You’re not allowed not to do it. You have to, by law, go after those people. And they made it like, ‘Oh, he was some kind of a Shylock-type guy.’”

Doctors have wide discretion on how to handle unpaid bills and are not required by law to sue patients or involve debt collectors.

“The term ‘Shylock’ is rooted in a longstanding antisemitic stereotype,” the Anti-Defamation League wrote Tuesday on social media, after The Times reached out to the Jewish advocacy group for comment on Mr. Trump’s remarks. “Regardless of intent, its use can reinforce harmful tropes about Jews and normalize language that has long been used to target the Jewish community.”

It was not the first time Mr. Trump has used the term publicly. During a rally last year in Iowa, he said that farmers should not have to go to, “in some cases, Shylocks and bad people” to borrow money. Afterward, Mr. Trump said he didn’t know it was an antisemitic slur.

“You view it differently than me,” Mr. Trump told reporters at the time. “I’ve never heard that.”

Jewish leaders and lawmakers last year quickly denounced his use of the term. The Anti-Defamation League called the trope “extremely offensive and dangerous.” Representative Jerry Nadler, Democrat of New York, said it was “one of the most recognizable antisemitic slurs in the English language.”

The Senate race in Kansas, which Republican leaders did not view as competitive just a few months ago, has evolved into one of the tightest contests of the midterm elections. Mr. Marshall faces Adam Hamilton, a megachurch pastor who is vying to become the first Democrat from Kansas elected to the Senate since 1932.

During the campaign, Mr. Hamilton has turned Mr. Marshall’s debt-collecting practices into fodder for political attacks and advertisements, one of which shows a former patient of Mr. Marshall’s saying she had been arrested while eight months pregnant for a $50 missed payment. Lawyers for Mr. Marshall called the ad “defamatory,” though Mr. Hamilton’s campaign continued to use it.

Other politicians have faced criticism for using the term “Shylock” in the past. In 2014, then-Vice President Joseph R. Biden Jr. apologized after he said it during a speech.

Mr. Trump’s comments come at a time when Republicans up and down the ballot, and across the country, have been trying to win over Jewish voters who feel disillusioned by the Democratic Party’s posture toward Israel. Republican leaders have seized on opportunities to draw a contrast on issues relating to Israel and antisemitism, often casting their Democratic opponents as threatening. Republican leaders have been relentless in their use of Islamophobic attacks against Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic candidate for Senate in Michigan, who is Muslim. Mr. Trump recently claimed that the candidate “hates Jews,” to which Dr. El-Sayed responded, “I love and revere Judaism and the Jewish people.”

Republican Senate candidates across the Midwest have struggled to make their case to voters amid rising energy prices and Mr. Trump’s unpopular war in Iran. Some, like Representative Ashley Hinson in Iowa and former Representative Mike Rogers in Michigan, have sought to distance themselves from the president on these issues. Mr. Marshall has not.

For years, Mr. Trump and his campaign have been accused of stealthily trying to win over racists and antisemites, a claim they reject. In 2016, Mr. Trump, then the presumptive Republican presidential nominee, posted an image on Twitter depicting Hillary Clinton beside a Jewish star and piles of money that had previously appeared on a message board known for antisemitism and white supremacy.

During Mr. Trump’s second term, official government social media accounts, including those for the White House, have made dozens of posts that invoke white supremacist and neo-Nazi messaging, drawing condemnation from Jewish leaders and experts in online extremism.

item.title: Bloomberg Gives Democrats $80 Million in 11th-Hour Midterm Push
item.description:
Around this time every election year, Democrats begin to wonder: Where is Michael R. Bloomberg?

And then, like clockwork, he makes his move — spending big money to help Democrats.

Mr. Bloomberg, the former New York City mayor and Democratic megadonor, is again serving as a late-arriving white knight for the party, sending about $80 million in September and October to help Democrats in the midterms, his team told The New York Times.

The giving, some of which is still underway, will make him one of the largest known left-leaning donors in the midterms. His team provided details on the donations before most of them show up in new campaign finance filings on Tuesday and Thursday.

“He believes in participation in our democracy,” Howard Wolfson, Mr. Bloomberg’s political adviser, said in an interview. “And obviously the scale of his participation, given his resources and his means, is greater than other people’s financially. But other people are participating in different ways.”

Will the money make a difference? After all, Mr. Bloomberg spent more than $1 billion on his own failed 2020 presidential campaign. “He is of the view that resources matter in campaigns,” Mr. Wolfson said.

Still, Mr. Wolfson said that Mr. Bloomberg, 84, who exited elected office more than a decade ago, “expects a result.”

Mr. Bloomberg is particularly focused on ensuring a sizable Democratic majority in the House of Representatives, the chamber that Democrats are most hopeful of flipping and that he tends to focus on. Mr. Bloomberg’s autumn budget is similar to what he spent during the fall 2018 campaign, which his team sees as the gold standard for when he was able to make an impact politically.

“Mayor Bloomberg played an incredibly instrumental role in the decisive midterm election in 2018,” Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the minority leader, said in a statement. “The extraordinary support from Mayor Bloomberg will once again help Democrats flip the House.”

At least $50 million of Mr. Bloomberg’s latest spending is headed to House races, including $24 million to Everytown for Gun Safety, a group he co-founded that is focused on the House this year. Another $16 million is going to House Majority PAC, the super PAC aligned with Mr. Jeffries. The money makes Mr. Bloomberg the largest disclosed donor for both groups.

Because Democrats are favored to win the House, big donors are sending more money to races for the Senate, which is seen as a tossup. Mr. Bloomberg wants Mr. Jeffries to have a governable majority — not just the 218 votes needed to become speaker.

“The difference between 221 and 230, in terms of the House majority, really matters,” Mr. Wolfson said, referring to how many seats Democrats could end up holding next year.

Mr. Bloomberg’s infusion of cash will offer some relief to Democrats who have watched apprehensively as Elon Musk and President Trump’s super PAC have unleashed hundreds of millions of dollars to support Republicans.

Much of Mr. Bloomberg’s largess has gone toward helping Democrats keep up with Republican spending on television and digital advertising across the country.

Mr. Wolfson said that Mr. Bloomberg remained deeply concerned about what he sees as the leftward drift of the Democratic Party, particularly on issues like Israel. Mr. Bloomberg is not “directing” money to left-wing supporters of the Democratic Socialists of America, Mr. Wolfson said.

Given his financial muscle and deeply held political views, Mr. Bloomberg is likely to play a role in helping to shape Democrats’ 2028 presidential primary race.

He has not made a decision on whom to support, Mr. Wolfson said, but one of Mr. Bloomberg’s donations this cycle backed Gov. Josh Shapiro of Pennsylvania, a potential Democratic candidate for president.

“He is a pragmatist. He is a centrist,” Mr. Wolfson said of Mr. Bloomberg. “I would be surprised if in the end he didn’t support someone who shared that orientation and was from that wing of the party.”

This year, around the time of Mr. Bloomberg’s donations, Everytown and House Majority PAC said they were working together on a roughly $10 million ad campaign for eight female House Democratic candidates who have worked on gun safety activism. Mr. Bloomberg’s funding of Everytown effectively freed up some of House Majority PAC’s money to be used elsewhere.

Mr. Bloomberg plans to soon spend an additional $10 million in House races, Mr. Wolfson said. During the spring, Mr. Bloomberg also spent $11 million to ensure that Assemblyman Micah Lasher emerged from a contentious primary to succeed Representative Jerrold Nadler of New York.

Since Sept. 1, Mr. Bloomberg has made other contributions, including $5 million to the super PAC allied with the League of Conservation Voters; $3.5 million total to a group focused on electing Democratic scientists and doctors; $2.5 million to a super PAC backing James Talarico, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Texas; and $8 million to help Democratic candidates for governor in half a dozen battleground states. Mr. Wolfson said Mr. Bloomberg also donated $2.5 million in September and October to a super PAC backing the re-election bid of Gov. Kathy Hochul of New York.

item.title: Attack Ad Featuring Candidate’s Mother Turns Ohio Governor’s Race Even Uglier
item.description:
A new attack ad in the Ohio governor's race features the mother of the Democratic candidate, Amy Acton — estranged from her daughter over allegations of molestation by a stepfather — calling the candidate a liar.

Republicans hailed the ad, which began circulating on social media Monday night, as a bombshell, while Democrats called it a new low by Dr. Acton’s opponent, Vivek Ramaswamy, in a campaign that was already one of the nation’s ugliest. Dr. Acton’s brother, Philip Stearns, condemned it as “a despicable low.”

Donna Arthur, Dr. Acton’s mother, says in the ad, “Don’t let her become your governor. If you think she’ll make your life better, you’re fooling yourself.”

On the campaign trail and during her time as the director of the Ohio Department of Health, Dr. Acton has shared details of a troubled childhood in which she was homeless for a time and was molested by her stepfather.

In 2019, Dr. Acton gave an interview to The Vindicator, the since-folded daily newspaper of Youngstown, Ohio, in which she disclosed being sexually abused between the ages of 9 and 12. In 1978, after her biological father made a report to the police, her stepfather was charged with rape and indicted by a grand jury. He pleaded not guilty.

In 2020, Ms. Arthur came forward to a conservative website to say her daughter’s claims of homelessness were exaggerated. Ms. Arthur shared that after her husband was arrested, Dr. Acton testified against him in court. Ms. Arthur supported her husband, rather than her daughter.

In the new ad, Ms. Arthur does not refer to the allegations of molestation. Instead, she dismisses Dr. Acton’s story that she lived in a tent as a child.

Both women have said that they have not seen or spoken to each other since that day in court in 1978.

Mr. Stearns, Dr. Acton’s brother, said in a statement Tuesday that he and his sister were removed from their mother’s custody after the arrest.

“Our birth mother stayed married to Amy’s rapist until he died,” Mr. Stearns said. “This desperate, disgusting attack reveals exactly who Vivek Ramaswamy is at his core — a pathetic excuse for a man who is willing to hurt anyone as long as it gets him what he wants.”

Mr. Ramaswamy’s campaign did not respond to substantive questions about the ad, including whether Ms. Arthur was paid to participate. And it is unclear if the ad came from Mr. Ramaswamy’s campaign or another organization that is backing his race.

But on Tuesday afternoon, amid a considerable backlash, Mr. Ramaswamy’s campaign appeared to endorse it.

“We don’t know what happened between Amy and her mother, who first spoke out about Amy in 2020, but we know that Amy Acton is a serial fabulist who has some serious problems with the truth,” Connie Luck, a spokeswoman for the Ramaswamy campaign, said in the statement.

Though the spot has gained traction on social media, including in an X post from Donald Trump Jr., it has not yet appeared on Ohio television, according to AdImpact.

Democrats have attacked Mr. Ramaswamy for a separate ad that a political website pointed out shows a man convicted of child sexual abuse. The spot was focused on a woman named Patty, who was nearly in tears over increases in property taxes and said she was afraid that she would lose her home. It showed Mr. Ramaswamy meeting Patty at a county fair, while her husband stood beside her.

Last week, The Bulwark reported that her husband was Vernon Edwards, a registered sex offender convicted in 2006 of “gross sexual imposition” with a victim under the age of 13.

Mr. Ramaswamy’s campaign later said it removed clips of Mr. Edwards from the ad, but according to AdImpact, the ad is still running unchanged.

Family members, such as President Trump’s niece Mary Trump, the siblings of Robert F. Kennedy Jr., and the siblings of Representative Paul Gosar, Republican of Arizona, have stepped forward in past campaigns to oppose their kin.

But few cases have been so visceral as the anti-Acton ad. Republicans had already attacked Dr. Acton in starkly personal terms, presenting her as a violent drunk, inflating the events of a single night in the Columbus, Ohio, suburbs in late August 2019 when police were dispatched to Dr. Acton’s house, but no charges were filed.

The Acton campaign has presented Mr. Ramaswamy as a con man and out-of-touch billionaire.

Whether yet another attack ad will have a meaningful impact on the race is unclear, said Melissa K. Miller, a Bowling Green State University professor who has been closely watching the race. This late in October, she said, voters are quick to tune out the endless political commercials on their televisions, and many have already made up their mind about who they want to be their next governor.

Campbell Robertson contributed reporting.

item.title: Richard Riehle, Prolific Actor Who Appeared in ‘Office Space,’ Dies at 78
item.description:
Richard Riehle, a prolific character actor best known for playing an anxious product manager in the 1999 film “Office Space,” died on Thursday. He was 78.

His representatives provided no other details about his death.

In a career that included more than 400 credits over several decades, Mr. Riehle performed in films, theater, television series, mini-series and even video games.

But Mr. Riehle was most likely best known for playing Tom Smykowski in “Office Space,” the cult classic and satire directed by Mike Judge about corporate employees being victimized by meaningless metrics, efficiency experts and other management fads.

Mr. Riehle’s character, Tom, is extremely anxious, terrified of losing his job at Initech, a tech company — which he eventually does. When corporate efficiency consultants interrogate Tom about what he does all day, he says:

Well — well look. I already told you: I deal with the goddamn customers so the engineers don’t have to. I have people skills; I am good at dealing with people. Can’t you understand that? What the hell is wrong with you people?

Tom later gets into a hit-and-run accident, leaving him in a full-body cast and wheelchair. After he receives a hefty settlement, he no longer needs to work.

Instead, he pursues his dream of creating a “Jump to Conclusions” floor mat, with squares with different conclusions that people can, literally, jump to.

How The Times decides who gets an obituary. There is no formula, scoring system or checklist in determining the news value of a life. We investigate, research and ask around before settling on our subjects. If you know of someone who might be a candidate for a Times obituary, please suggest it here.

“This is a horrible idea,” one of his colleagues tells him.

Richard Riehle was born on May 12, 1948 in Menomonee Falls, Wis. His father, Herbert John Riehle, was an assistant postmaster, and his mother, Mary Margaret, was a nurse. His father died when he was 13.

As the oldest of six children, Mr. Riehle worked 40 hours a week at a grocery store to help support his family.

He participated in high school plays, but after graduation he entered a seminary to become a priest. After getting caught sneaking back to the seminary from seeing “Lawrence of Arabia” without permission, he decided that the priesthood was not for him.

“They sat me down at that point and just asked me if I really thought this was the right place for me,” he told Notre Dame Magazine in 2011. “We both knew the answer.”

Mr. Riehle attended the University of Notre Dame, where he acted, directed and built sets. He became fluent in German during a study abroad program in Austria.

After graduating from Notre Dame in 1970, he became a teaching assistant at the University of Minnesota, where he earned a master’s degree in fine arts and began his professional stage career, spending years working in regional theater. He also took on small screen roles.

“I was content during that time,” Mr. Riehle told his alumni magazine. “I always seemed to find work.”

He made his debut on Broadway in “Execution of Justice” in 1986, and stayed in New York for another decade, later appearing in “The Iceman Cometh” in 1999, alongside Paul Giamatti. He appeared in dozens of TV shows, including “Hot Pursuit,” “L.A. Law,” “Quantum Leap,” “Murder, She Wrote” and “The West Wing.”

He even appeared in the soap opera “One Life to Live,” and played a high school principal in a TV adaptation of “Ferris Bueller’s Day Off.”

“I always wanted the role that would bring something out of me, force me to find something extra,” Mr. Riehle told his alumni magazine. “The lead isn’t always the best part in a play or a movie.”

His breakthrough in film occurred in 1989, when he played a bureaucratic quartermaster in the Civil War drama “Glory.” Roles in more than 100 films followed, including the “The Fugitive,” “Casino,” and playing parts in three “Star Trek” franchises.

“Beyond his immense talent, he will be remembered for his genuine goodness, boundless kindness, and unwavering generosity, particularly toward emerging actors and filmmakers, whom he encouraged and supported at every opportunity,” his talent agency, Artists & Representatives, and management company, Wright Entertainment, said in a joint statement.

Complete information on survivors was not immediately available.

Mr. Riehle has parts in approximately another dozen films that are in production, or that have been completed.

Kitty Bennett contributed research.

]]>

item.title: As Trump Wages Golf Course Fight, Many Residents Fear What Could Be Lost
item.description:
On Monday morning, as an exasperated federal judge was demanding that the Trump administration abide by her orders, Noah Mihalovic, 4, was chasing a little yellow golf ball across the mini-golf course at East Potomac Park.

Noah had come to the park in Washington, D.C., with his mother, Caroline Mihalovic. She used to come here in her younger days and once ran around it in the annual Cherry Blossom 10-mile race. Now she had brought her son to what is, for now, the oldest continuously operating mini-golf course in the country for what might be a last round if the president gets his way.

“I heard that things potentially might get demolished, or renovated,” Ms. Mihalovic lamented. “I wanted to get him out here to experience the old-school course.”

For months, President Trump has been trumpeting his plan to fully revamp the East Potomac Golf Links, a historic 36-hole facility that lies on an okra-shaped spit of land in the Potomac River. The course takes up most of the island but shares it with other features long enjoyed by people in the area, including the mini-golf course, a bike trail, a playground and a picnic area.

Vowing to make the golf links “one of the Most Wonderful and Spectacular Golf Courses anywhere in the World,” Mr. Trump has insisted a full renovation begin immediately, the latest project in his extreme D.C. makeover.

Hundreds of trees have already been cut down, though the administration’s lawyers said this was routine maintenance. And while preservationists continue to fight the plan in court, Mr. Trump, who early Tuesday morning posted a slew of photographs of things needing repair on the current course, which he referred to as “Trash Island,” has unveiled a proposal for his vision on social media.

This plan notably leaves out almost everything but a clubhouse, a driving range and single 18-hole course.

East Potomac, like the two other public golf courses in Washington, has had maintenance issues over the years, including serious drainage problems. Even the mayor of Washington, Muriel Bowser, acknowledged that some attention is due. “You won’t be surprised that I think all of the golf courses need rehabilitation,” she said in a news briefing on Monday morning. “They’re federal golf courses, and they should be rehabilitated.”

But the East Potomac property, as the mayor also alluded to in her remarks, encompasses more than just another golf course.

With easy access for city residents and low greens fees, East Potomac Golf Links has been known by many as the “people’s country club,” where working-class Black Washingtonians would come to play golf and socialize. As Washington has gentrified over the years, the democratic nature of the course has waned somewhat. But it is still inexpensive, and it is still nearby.

“Everyone who comes here says this is one of the greatest things that D.C. has, like a public course this close to the District as cheap as it is and decent quality,” said Michael Peterkin, 49, who was making his way through a bucket of balls at the driving range. “Certainly, good enough golf.”

And there is more to it than the course. Every day, hundreds of runners, walkers and cyclists follow the route around the links, looping the grassy common at the park’s tip, known as Hains Point. Here, families settle down for noonday picnics, and fishermen come to cast rods in the evening.

Groups have gathered for generations of family reunions and long summer afternoon cookouts. Children come to climb and slide at the playground, or play the mini-golf course, where on Monday Noah Mihalovic scored a hole in one.

And there are hundreds of maples, birches, cherry blossoms, oaks and other trees, if fewer than there were a few weeks ago.

“I’m worried about the trees,” said Anoa Gibson, 39, a medic at a construction site near the entrance to the park. She had trained for a triathlon here, putting in miles on the bike path around the park. But she also just enjoys sitting in the quiet on her lunch break. “These trees, some of them are like 100 years old,” she said. “That’s what I’m most concerned about.”

In an interview on Fox News’s “America Reports” on Monday, Doug Burgum, the U.S. secretary of the interior, said that removing trees was “restoring it back to its historical nature,” referring to photos of the course in the 1920s that showed presidents golfing with “barely a tree” around. He also insisted the course would remain public after the renovation.

“It could be the best course in America with the lowest prices,” he said.

At the hearing on Monday, Judge Ana C. Reyes, a federal judge who Mr. Trump has said “may be insane” and whom the administration is trying to get removed from the case, grilled the lawyers from the Justice Department, saying it looked as if the Trump administration was simply moving forward with the overhaul even as officials had sworn that no decisions had been made.

“The disturbing thing about how this administration goes about things is, they don’t ask permission,” Mr. Peterkin said. It’s just rolling over people, he added, “not caring what they think, what they want.”

Chuck Thies, a political consultant based in D.C., is discouraged by the whole debate. The main course at East Potomac is not in great shape, he said, and a sports-obsessed city like Washington, which in recent years has furiously and successfully fought to keep its pro basketball team and bring home its pro football team, could use one championship-level golf course. At the same time, Hains Point really is a city treasure, he said, as are the bike path and many of the old trees.

“There’s room for 18 holes and a bike path and a place to barbecue,” he said. “The problem here is the politics.”

A little after lunchtime, Barbara McCann, 55, was making what she called “a prayer circle” around the park, riding her bike on the loop that nearly encircles the golf course. She had spent the first part of the day a couple of miles north, in U.S. District Court, watching Judge Reyes and the lawyers spar over the fate of the park she was now circling.

This whole plan was autocratic, she had concluded, unthinkable, the destruction of a beloved public treasure by the greed of the wealthy. But perhaps more than that: It was an odd thing for the leader of the free world to be so focused on.

“Doesn’t he have better things to do?” she asked.
